claims.text: The initial material is a polycrystalline HfNbTaTiZr high-entropy alloy.
Combining systematic experimental alloying with molecular dynamics simulations can predict and validate the effects of elemental percentages on the mechanical properties of HfNbTaTiZr.
The proposed intervention varies the percentages of Hf, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr systematically.
Mechanical testing is to be performed at room temperature using tensile and compression tests.
Changes in elemental percentages affect grain size.
Changes in elemental percentages affect lattice strain.
Changes in elemental percentages affect atomic-scale defects.
Elucidating composition-structure-property relationships permits constituent-specific effects on strength, ductility, and toughness to be predicted and validated.
Increasing Ti by 10% and decreasing Hf by 5% will increase yield strength by 10-20% relative to the stated baseline.
Increasing Ti by 10% and decreasing Hf by 5% will increase ductility by 5-10% relative to the stated baseline.
The predicted outcome is valid for elemental-composition variations of 10-30%.
Prediction accuracy depends on the accuracy of the molecular dynamics simulations and experimental alloying process.
The hypothesis is falsified if measured yield strength and ductility for the modified alloy are not within 5% of the predicted values.

contradictions.description: If the subscripts in Hf25Nb25Ta25Ti25Zr25 are intended as atomic percentages, they sum to 125%, so the baseline is not a valid percentage composition. The proposed Ti increase and Hf decrease also do not define a mass-balanced modified composition.

The outcome is specified as broad ranges, but the falsification rule requires measurements to be within 5% of 'the predicted values' without defining a single target value or how distance from a range is calculated.
